To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the default MOE for inter- and intraspecies uncertainty factor is more protective when it is based on a comparison of parent blood concentrations between humans and animals than on a comparison of external doses.
the default MOE based on an external dose may not provide sufficient protection if applied on a basis of blood concentrations.

the default MOE based on an external dose of 100 is generally more protective than a default MOE of unity based on a blood concentration of parent compound in the laboratory species, and that a default MOE based upon a blood concentration of 1 in the human is generally more protective that a default MOEs of 100 or unity based on external dose.
In summary, our research is concerned with

whether the default MOEs applied to risk assessments of volatile organic compounds are protective when based on comparisons of measured blood concentrations of parent compounds in humans compared to laboratory animal species.
the application of a default uncertainty factor to account for inter-species and inter-individual variability in toxicokinetics.
developing a new approach that could provide a more protective margin of exposure for chemicals that have been assessed using a physiologically based pharmacokinetic model.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the default MOE based on blood concentrations is protective and may be applied to the blood concentration of parent compound of a chemical.

, depending upon the chemical characteristics and the toxicokinetic model, a default MOE based on comparative blood concentrations could be more protective or less protective than a default MOE applied to external doses.
the default MOE based on blood concentrations is protective, but the degree of protection is dependent on the chemical characteristics and the conditions under which the MOE is applied.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the default MOE is protective for most chemicals, but the default MOE could be relaxed for some classes of compounds.
for chemicals with similar characteristics, the default MOEs are more protective when applied based on blood concentrations than on external doses.
the default target MOEs of 100 applied to external doses are generally protective when applied to blood concentrations.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the default MOE based on blood concentrations may be more protective than that based on external dose for certain chemicals, but that this is dependent on chemical-specific properties, the route of administration, and the point of departure.

for chemicals with characteristics similar to the generic model used in the analysis, MOE based on blood concentration comparisons between laboratory animals and people can provide a useful alternative to the default MOE based on an external dose comparison.

, in some cases, the default MOEs of 100 and 10 for inter- and intraspecies extrapolation, respectively, are not needed to ensure adequate protection of human health, and that the use of a default MOE of only 10 for interspecies extrapolation may be appropriate for some chemicals.
